newsitem.title: USA: Clouds seen as a cause of global warming.
newsitem.headline: Clouds seen as a cause of global warming.

text.p: Clouds may have more of an impact on global warming than urbanization, the weekly magazine Science reported on Thursday.

The finding was the result of a new study of global warming that took into account temperatures in the generally cloudier Southern Hemisphere, which traditionally is left out of global temperature records, Science reported.

"The trends we're seeing on (higher) minimum temperatures are a result of cloud increases, certainly more than urbanization factors," David R. Easterling, the lead author of the Science article, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
He also said the global trend toward increased cloudiness is an unresolved question that requires further study.
Experts found that temperatures in the more rural Southern Hemisphere have been rising along with temperatures in the more industrialised Northern Hemisphere.

World surface temperatures have risen an average of 0.5 degrees Celsius during the 20th century, a phenomenon largely attributed to an increase in so-called "greenhouse gas" emissions caused by industrialisation and deforestation.
"It's very likely a combination of some natural fluctuations, but also very definitely human industrialisation globally," Easterling said. "The real difficult thing is separating the two."
Science reported that higher average temperatures are largely due to higher minimum temperatures.
Increased cloudiness acts like a blanket that traps in nighttime heat, contributing to higher nighttime temperatures, when most minimum temperatures occur.

The team of investigators analysed monthly temperature averages at 5,400 observing stations around the world, covering 54 percent of the earth's land surface, 17 percent more than previous studies, Science reported.
Most of the temperature increases were in the Southern Hemisphere, which is more rural and less industrial than the Northern Hemisphere.
The temperatures recorded at 4,100 rural stations showed only slight differences from those recorded at all 5,400 stations.
"However, there are still large parts of the world that remain unanalyzed because of a lack of data, particularly in the tropics, and updating these data remains a problem," the Science article said.
